paragraphs: Managers often justify continuing a failing project by pointing to the money already spent on it. The reasoning feels natural but is flawed, because that money is gone whether the project continues or stops; the only relevant question is whether the further expenditure required will be repaid by future returns. Economists call the earlier outlay a sunk cost, and the discipline of ignoring it is easier to endorse than to practice. Part of the difficulty is that abandoning a project crystallizes a loss that was previously only prospective, and part is that a manager who cancels a project may be judged to have admitted a mistake. Organizations that reward candid reassessment, rather than stubborn persistence, tend to make such decisions better.
